questions.q: What is a OneLake shortcut, per this lesson?
options: A reference inside a Lakehouse that points at data living elsewhere, without physically copying it
A keyboard shortcut for navigating the Fabric admin portal
A compressed backup copy of a table
A deprecated feature replaced by OneLake Catalog
questions.explain: A shortcut looks like a normal folder inside the Lakehouse, but every read resolves through to the real, external location.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say shortcuts matter specifically for governance?
options: The data you're governing might physically sit in a completely different subscription or cloud provider than the workspace suggests
Shortcuts are only available to Fabric administrators
Shortcuts automatically bypass all access control
Shortcuts cannot be created inside a Lakehouse
questions.explain: Access control, data residency, and classification all have to account for this indirection, not just the folder structure visible inside Fabric.

questions.q: How does a shortcut appear in Fabric's lineage view, per this lesson?
options: As a real dependency edge, drawn exactly like any other connection such as a dataflow or pipeline
It never appears in lineage view at all
Only as a text footnote, not a visual connection
Only if the shortcut points to another Fabric workspace
questions.explain: A shortcut is a genuine data dependency, not a special invisible case — lineage view draws it as a real edge.

questions.q: What does enabling shortcut caching do, according to this lesson?
options: Stores a copy of recently-accessed shortcut data inside OneLake for a configurable retention period of 1-28 days
Permanently deletes the original source data
Disables all lineage tracking for that shortcut
Automatically grants read access to every workspace member
questions.explain: Caching is workspace-level, with its own retention window and a manual reset option — and the cached copy persists independently of the source.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call shortcut caching a governance consideration, not just a performance one?
options: A cached copy exists independently of the source for up to 28 days, so a deletion or access revocation at the source doesn't automatically clear it
Caching is always disabled by default and cannot be changed
Caching only affects how fast queries run, with no other implications
Caching automatically enforces data retention policies
questions.explain: This is exactly the kind of gap a data retention policy needs to account for — the cache can outlive the access rights that originally justified it.
